title: Megh Aaye
author: Sarveshwar Dayal Saxena
tagline: The monsoon as homecoming: clouds arrive dressed as guests and the whole village rises to welcome them.

overview.intro: Sarveshwar Dayal Saxena’s "Megh Aaye" ("The Clouds Have Come") turns the arrival of the monsoon into a village welcome. The clouds come dressed up like guests from the city; the breeze leads the greeting and doors and windows open through the lanes; trees crane their necks, the river pauses behind its veil, the old peepal steps forward to salute, and a waiting vine complains that it was remembered only after a year. The delighted pond offers a platter of water, lightning flashes across a courtyard sky, and when the embankment finally breaks, the rain pours down like tears of reunion. Sustained personification makes weather behave like a community.

learn.title: The clouds come dressed as guests

blocks.text: The poem opens on an entrance. The clouds arrive all dressed up and adorned, and Saxena’s simile immediately tells us how to read them: like guests coming from a city into a village. That single comparison sets the entire poem’s terms, because guests are not weather — they are expected, welcomed and greeted, and their arrival reorganises the life of the house. Here the house is a whole village, and every element of it takes a role in the greeting.

The breeze leads the welcome, and doors and windows open through the lanes. Note how physical the response is: the village does not observe the monsoon, it opens itself to it. From the first stanza the poem insists that nature and community are not separate categories, and it prepares the reader for a series of greetings in which each feature of the landscape behaves like a neighbour.

items: Trees crane their necks to look, straining to see the guests approach.
The storm lifts the dust like a woman’s skirt, a domestic and playful image.
The river pauses and glances coyly from behind its veil, as a shy bride might.
The old peepal steps forward and offers the traditional greeting of respect.
A vine waiting by the door complains that it was remembered only after a year.

blocks.text: Each greeting has its own character, and the variety is the point. The trees are eager, the river modest, the peepal formally respectful, the vine reproachful. Saxena is doing more than decorating the scene: he is giving the landscape a set of personalities so that the monsoon’s arrival registers as a social event with moods, obligations and small grievances — exactly the texture of a real homecoming.

items.meaning: The arriving guests, dressed and adorned, at the centre of every greeting.
items.context: Their arrival reorganises the village’s behaviour, as honoured guests do.

items.context: It acts as the herald announcing the guests’ approach.

items.meaning: The aged tree that steps forward to offer a formal salutation.
items.context: It represents the village’s elders paying respectful welcome.

items.meaning: The plant at the door that complains of being remembered late.
items.context: It supplies the one note of reproach in an otherwise delighted welcome.

items.meaning: The delighted body of water that brings out a platter of water.
items.context: Its offering is the welcome’s most generous gesture.

blocks.text: Reading the cast together shows Saxena’s design. The breeze heralds, the trees are eager, the river shy, the peepal respectful, the vine reproachful and the pond generous. This is a full social hierarchy at work, which is why the poem feels less like description than like a piece of village theatre staged for honoured guests.

blocks.caption: The stages of the welcome
rows: The clouds arrive dressed; the breeze leads; doors open
Guests announced at the village edge
Trees crane, river veils, peepal salutes, vine complains
Neighbours each offering their own welcome
The pond brings out a platter of water
Lightning flashes; the embankment breaks; rain pours
Tears of joy at a meeting long delayed

blocks.text: The poem’s climax arrives when the embankment breaks and the rain pours down in streams, described as the tears of reunion. The image completes the conceit: if the clouds are guests and the village is family, then the rain is what finally releases the emotion everyone has been performing. The withheld feeling of the earlier stanzas — the greeting, the offering, the reproach — resolves into an outpouring, and the personification earns its ending.

The poem’s governing device is personification, but it is sustained rather than occasional, and that is what makes it work. A single metaphor would decorate a description; a consistent one transforms the event, because every new detail is obliged to stay in character. The trees must behave like neighbours, the river like a modest woman, the pond like a generous host — and once that law is established, the reader accepts each fresh greeting without surprise.

blocks.text: This poem reliably produces questions on personification, on the central idea, and on the significance of the ending. Prepare by learning the order of the welcome — breeze, trees, river, peepal, vine, pond, rain — since answers that cite the sequence in order are always clearer than those that list images at random. Keep the reunion reading of the final line firmly in view; it is what turns a weather poem into a poem about belonging.

questions.prompt: How does the poem describe the arriving clouds?
options: Dressed up and adorned, like guests from a city
questions.answer: Dressed up and adorned, like guests from a city
questions.explanation: The opening image presents the clouds as guests arriving dressed and adorned, which sets the terms for the whole poem’s welcome.
questions.commonMistake: The clouds are festive guests, not a looming storm.

questions.prompt: What leads the welcome of the clouds?
options: The breeze, which opens doors and windows
questions.answer: The breeze, which opens doors and windows
questions.explanation: The breeze heralds the guests’ approach, and doors and windows open through the lanes in response.
questions.commonMistake: The wind acts as the herald rather than as a character among the greeters.

questions.prompt: Who offers a traditional greeting to the clouds?
questions.explanation: The aged peepal steps forward and offers the respectful salutation, taking the role of the village’s elders.
questions.commonMistake: Each character has a distinct role; the peepal greets formally, others differently.

questions.prompt: What does the waiting vine do as the clouds arrive?
options: It complains that it was remembered after a year
questions.answer: It complains that it was remembered after a year
questions.explanation: The vine supplies the welcome’s single note of reproach, which gives the scene the realism of an actual family greeting.
questions.commonMistake: The complaint is affectionate rather than hostile.

questions.prompt: What offering does the pond make to the clouds?
questions.answer: The delighted pond brings out a platter full of water as its welcome.
questions.explanation: The pond’s generous offering is the hospitality gesture of the scene, matching the mood of a household honouring its guests.
questions.commonMistake: Describe it as an offering of hospitality, not merely as water rising.

questions.prompt: How does the poem describe the river as the clouds arrive?
questions.answer: The river pauses and glances coyly from behind its veil, like a modest bride.
questions.explanation: Saxena gives the river modesty and self-consciousness, so the natural feature behaves like a person aware of being seen.
questions.commonMistake: The image is of shyness behind a veil, not of the river flooding or stopping.

questions.prompt: Explain how personification is sustained across the poem and what it achieves.
questions.answer: The poem’s governing device is personification, but it is sustained rather than occasional. The clouds are guests dressed for a visit; the breeze is the herald who opens the doors; the trees crane their necks like eager neighbours; the river glances from behind its veil like a shy bride; the old peepal offers the respectful salutation of an elder; the vine complains like a slighted friend; and the pond carries out a platter of water like a generous host. Because every detail keeps to its assigned social role, the monsoon ceases to be weather and becomes a village event with moods and obligations. The effect is to make nature and community inseparable, so the reader experiences the rain not as a change in the sky but as the arrival of family.
questions.explanation: Enumerate the roles in sequence, then state what the consistency achieves — weather transformed into a social occasion.
questions.commonMistake: Do not merely list examples; show that the device is sustained and that this consistency is what produces the effect.

questions.prompt: What does the final image of rain as reunion’s tears suggest?
questions.answer: That the pouring rain releases the emotion the whole welcome had been performing — the joy of a meeting long delayed.
questions.explanation: When the embankment breaks and the rain streams down, the withheld feeling of the greetings resolves into an outpouring, completing the conceit of guests and family.
questions.commonMistake: Read the ending emotionally rather than literally as a description of heavy rain.

questions.prompt: Describe the arrival of the clouds and show how the poem makes a natural event feel like a homecoming.
questions.answer: The clouds arrive dressed up and adorned, and the poem’s simile immediately compares them to guests coming from a city into a village. The breeze leads the welcome, opening doors and windows through the lanes. Each feature of the landscape then greets them in character: the trees crane their necks to look, the storm lifts the dust like a woman’s skirt, the river pauses and glances coyly from behind its veil, the old peepal steps forward to offer a respectful salutation, and the waiting vine complains that it was remembered only after a year. The delighted pond brings out a platter of water, and lightning flashes as the horizon widens into a deep courtyard. Finally the embankment breaks and the rain pours down like the tears of reunion. By sustaining personification across every detail — herald, eager neighbours, modest bride, elder, reproachful friend, generous host — Saxena turns weather into a social occasion, so the monsoon is experienced not as a change in the sky but as the return of family.
questions.explanation: Follow the sequence in order and close on the reunion reading, so the answer reconstructs both the conceit and its emotional logic.
questions.commonMistake: Do not present the images as a random list; the greeting order is what proves the welcome is staged like a homecoming.

questions.prompt: The poem treats nature as a welcoming community. Does this way of seeing the monsoon still make sense today? Discuss.
questions.answer: Saxena’s personification still makes sense because it names something real: the monsoon is not mere weather in an agricultural village but an event on which the year depends, and expectation, welcome and relief genuinely attend it. The dressed clouds, the opened doors and the tears of reunion are exact emotional descriptions of what a delayed rainspall feels like, whether one reads the field or the water tank. At the same time, a modern reader may notice how much the poem depends on a shared communal life — the vine’s complaint and the peepal’s salutation assume neighbours who know one another. That is not a weakness but a record of a relationship with nature that cities have thinned. The poem therefore does double duty: it preserves an older intimacy and asks whether something has been lost in the way we now meet the season.
questions.explanation: Take a clear position — the seeing still works, and its value is partly elegiac — and ground it in the poem’s specific images before adding the modern qualification.
questions.commonMistake: Do not dismiss the personification as primitive fancy; engage with why the emotion it describes is accurate.
